vignette:
At 26 years old, Clara found herself grappling with the haunting remnants of a traumatic experience that had altered her life as a firefighter. It had been a routine call, a blaze in an abandoned warehouse, when she and her team had become trapped by a sudden backdraft. The intense heat had felt like a living thing, wrapping around her as she fought to escape, but the chaos of the fire had quickly turned to an overwhelming sensation of suffocation and fear. In the aftermath, she had been freed, but the memories of that experience clung to her like smoke in her lungs. Now, Clara’s life was filled with vivid recollections that felt more real than anything else, often invading her thoughts unexpectedly and leaving her disoriented, as if the events were happening all over again.

Clara's world had shrunk significantly since that day. Crowded spaces, like the bustling fire station during shift changes, became unbearable, triggering a wave of panic that would send her heart racing. The sound of laughter and chatter that once filled her with camaraderie now felt oppressive, a reminder of the bonds she had lost in her mind. In those moments, Clara would think to herself, “This is what your life is now — flinching at nothing,” as the laughter served as a painful reminder of her perceived failures and her growing sense of isolation. In those moments, the laughter triggered memories of her colleagues, amplifying her feelings of isolation and deepening her sense of loss, pulling her back into the chaos of the fire as if it were happening all over again. The laughter would evoke vivid images of the day of the fire, as if each sound brought with it the heat and chaos she had experienced, making her feel as if she were once again trapped in that moment. Each time those memories surfaced, they solidified her belief that she was weak and incapable, leading her to think, “I can’t handle this,” further embedding the idea that she wasn’t cut out for the job. When she stumbled upon old photographs from her training days, the images would suddenly evoke a flood of memories, each one feeling as though it belonged to someone else, almost alien in quality. Clara often found herself standing frozen, staring at the faces of her colleagues, grappling with an identity that felt increasingly elusive. She would think, “This is me? I don’t even recognize myself anymore.”

As time passed, Clara began to notice that her self-view was heavily intertwined with her memories of the fire. The belief that she was weak made each recollection of the fire more potent, as if her perceived failures were magnified with every flashback, reinforcing her sense of inadequacy. Each time she failed to act as she thought a firefighter should—calm and collected—she would berate herself, believing that her perceived inadequacies had led to her entrapment. This conviction that she was weak fed directly into her memories of the fire, making each recollection sharper and more painful, as if she was not just remembering but reliving her failure. Her belief that she was weak transformed these memories into vivid reminders of her inadequacies, amplifying her sense of threat as she felt herself becoming trapped in the very chaos she sought to escape. Her belief that she was weak made her memories feel like constant reminders of her inadequacies, reinforcing the narrative that she would always be vulnerable and unable to cope. The weight of those vividly painful memories further convinced Clara that she was incapable, deepening her negative self-appraisal as she relived moments of perceived weakness. Each recollection made her feel more vulnerable, reinforcing her belief that she was fundamentally broken and unworthy of safety, which in turn heightened her sense of threat in every aspect of her life. Each time the memories returned, they brought with them a wave of shame that solidified her view of herself as someone who was fundamentally broken and unworthy of safety. The belief that she was weak transformed her memories into vivid reminders of her perceived inadequacies, amplifying the pain and fear associated with each flashback and making her feel even more vulnerable. This self-blame spiraled into a deeper anxiety, making her feel even less capable of coping with the pressures of her job and daily life. Clara's belief that she had failed her team made every new challenge seem insurmountable, filling her with an overwhelming sense of threat that any misstep would prove her weaknesses — a certainty that left her constantly braced for danger. She started avoiding situations that might trigger her memories, convinced that any slip-up would confirm her fears that she was not cut out for this profession. The persistent sense of threat made her hyper-aware of every situation, turning ordinary moments into potential triggers that could unleash her memories of the fire. With the constant threat in her mind, she began to see danger in every unfamiliar face and environment, convinced that any misstep could lead to a recurrence of her past trauma. The more she avoided, the more she felt like a shadow of her former self, deepening the cycle of negative thoughts. Her conviction that she was not cut out for the job led her to see danger everywhere, making even the most mundane situations feel like potential threats that could trigger her memories. Her belief that she was incapable made the memories of the fire feel like a constant threat lurking around every corner, reinforcing her conviction that she was not safe, even in familiar surroundings.

The intrusive memories that Clara experienced were not just fleeting images; they were often accompanied by a visceral sense of threat. Even in safe environments, she struggled to relax, her body always on high alert, as if danger were lurking just around the corner. The heightened sense of threat kept her dwelling on her traumatic memories, as if she needed to remain vigilant to avoid reliving those moments of chaos and fear. vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette does not establish a causal connection between triggers and memory, as it describes triggers but does not explain how they specifically lead to intrusive memories.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette lacks a causal relationship between negative appraisals and threat, failing to show how Clara's negative beliefs contribute to her feelings of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: There is no connection shown where negative appraisals lead to memory, as it does not indicate how her negative beliefs influence her memories of the trauma.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Threat: The relationship between memory and threat is not made clear; while memories provoke a sense of threat, the vignette does not explicitly show how memory leads to that feeling of threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not clarify how the sense of threat informs or affects Clara's memories, missing the connection from threat to memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
At 26 years old, Clara found herself grappling with the haunting remnants of a traumatic experience that had altered her life as a firefighter. It had been a routine call, a blaze in an abandoned warehouse, when she and her team had become trapped by a sudden backdraft. The intense heat had felt like a living thing, wrapping around her as she fought to escape, but the chaos of the fire had quickly turned to an overwhelming sensation of suffocation and fear. In the aftermath, she had been freed, but the memories of that experience clung to her like smoke in her lungs. Now, Clara’s life was filled with vivid recollections that felt more real than anything else, often invading her thoughts unexpectedly and leaving her disoriented, as if the events were happening all over again.

Clara's world had shrunk significantly since that day. Crowded spaces, like the bustling fire station during shift changes, became unbearable, triggering a wave of panic that would send her heart racing. The sound of laughter and chatter that once filled her with camaraderie now felt oppressive, a reminder of the bonds she had lost in her mind. In those moments, the laughter triggered memories of her colleagues, amplifying her feelings of isolation and deepening her sense of loss, pulling her back into the chaos of the fire as if it were happening all over again. The laughter would evoke vivid images of the day of the fire, as if each sound brought with it the heat and chaos she had experienced, making her feel as if she were once again trapped in that moment. When she stumbled upon old photographs from her training days, the images would suddenly evoke a flood of memories, each one feeling as though it belonged to someone else, almost alien in quality. Clara often found herself standing frozen, staring at the faces of her colleagues, grappling with an identity that felt increasingly elusive. She would think, “This is me? I don’t even recognize myself anymore.”

As time passed, Clara began to notice that her self-view was heavily intertwined with her memories of the fire. The belief that she was weak made each recollection of the fire more potent, as if her perceived failures were magnified with every flashback, reinforcing her sense of inadequacy. Each time she failed to act as she thought a firefighter should—calm and collected—she would berate herself, believing that her perceived inadequacies had led to her entrapment. This conviction that she was weak fed directly into her memories of the fire, making each recollection sharper and more painful, as if she was not just remembering but reliving her failure. The weight of those vividly painful memories further convinced Clara that she was incapable, deepening her negative self-appraisal as she relived moments of perceived weakness. The belief that she was weak transformed her memories into vivid reminders of her perceived inadequacies, amplifying the pain and fear associated with each flashback and making her feel even more vulnerable. This self-blame spiraled into a deeper anxiety, making her feel even less capable of coping with the pressures of her job and daily life. Clara's belief that she had failed her team made every new challenge seem insurmountable, filling her with an overwhelming sense of threat that any misstep would prove her weaknesses — a certainty that left her constantly braced for danger. She started avoiding situations that might trigger her memories, convinced that any slip-up would confirm her fears that she was not cut out for this profession. The persistent sense of threat made her hyper-aware of every situation, turning ordinary moments into potential triggers that could unleash her memories of the fire. The more she avoided, the more she felt like a shadow of her former self, deepening the cycle of negative thoughts. Her belief that she was incapable made the memories of the fire feel like a constant threat lurking around every corner, reinforcing her conviction that she was not safe, even in familiar surroundings.

The intrusive memories that Clara experienced were not just fleeting images; they were often accompanied by a visceral sense of threat. Even in safe environments, she struggled to relax, her body always on high alert, as if danger were lurking just around the corner. The sound of a door slamming or a loud engine revving would send her jumping, her heart racing as if she were back in that warehouse, fighting for air. The memories would flood back, each one more vivid than the last, creating a churning pit of anxiety within her that felt impossible to escape. Once the memories surfaced, they brought with them an overwhelming sense of danger that felt immediate, as though the trauma was still happening, leaving her to grapple with the sensations of fear and helplessness that accompanied them. Once the memories surfaced, they brought with them an overwhelming sense of danger that felt immediate; she was no longer safe in her own mind, and the threat felt as if it were still present, looming just out of reach. The memories of the fire, once triggered, left Clara feeling hunted, as if the danger she had experienced was not just a past event but something that still encircled her. Clara began to fear that the act of remembering was a sign of her fragility, confirming all her worst fears. The constant fear of reliving those moments reinforced her belief that she was not resilient, solidifying the idea that she was permanently altered by her trauma.

In her current state, Clara felt trapped in a loop of fear and shame. This loop was fueled by the persistent sense of threat that followed her, leading her to accept that she was forever vulnerable and incapable of escaping her past. Her memories of the fire—so real and so vivid—had morphed into a source of constant dread. She could feel how they influenced her, tightening their grip with every recollection that surfaced. The more she tried to push them away, the more powerful they became, leading her to withdraw from her colleagues and activities that once brought her joy. This persistent sense of threat kept her entrenched in her memories, as if the act of remembering was a necessary defense against the danger she believed was always just around the corner. She had come to dread the quiet moments when the memories would resurface, reminding her of her perceived failures. It was as if she was caught in a cycle where every memory only deepened her sense of isolation, and with each cycle, she felt her grip on reality slipping further away.

Now, sitting in a therapist's office, Clara felt a mix of fear and hope. She was terrified that she might never regain the sense of self she had lost, but the thought of continuing to live in this torment was even scarier. She hoped to reclaim her life, to find a way to navigate the world without the constant weight of her memories crushing her spirit. Clara feared that without help, the memories would continue to loom over her, reinforcing her belief that she was fragile and unable to handle the challenges of her life. “I just want to feel like myself again,” she whispered, her voice tinged with vulnerability. Clara knew she needed help to break free from the chains of the past, to learn how to live again, and to find a way to make peace with her memories rather than letting them define her. Every time she found herself in a crowded space, the panic would trigger vivid memories of the fire, as if the noise and chaos were pulling her back into that moment of entrapment.
